How a 16-Year-Old Student Passed His GCSEs Using Eye-Tracking Technology — and the Systemic Hurdles He Faced

29 Oct 2026, 02:22 AM IST · GlobeWire Daily Education Desk · Source: www.theguardian.com

A Remarkable Academic Milestone

Patrick McCabe, a 16-year-old student with cerebral palsy, has successfully passed all seven of his GCSEs at Fallibroome Academy in Macclesfield, Cheshire. Using specialised eye-tracking (Eyegaze) technology and an augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) device, Patrick completed his exams over a grueling four-month period. Having achieved the grades necessary to continue into the sixth form, he has now begun studying A-levels in French, business, and media studies.

Patrick has attended local mainstream schools since his family moved back to England from Switzerland when he was six years old. Reflecting on his education using his AAC device, he noted that learning alongside his peers allowed him to develop skills and an independent mind, much like his older brothers.

The Rigors of Eye-Tracking Assessments

While Patrick's academic achievement is a testament to his determination, the process highlighted significant barriers in the current examination system for students with special educational needs and disabilities (Send). Because of the time required to communicate via eye-tracking technology, Patrick's exam schedule stretched from 2 February until 5 June, running every morning while his peers revised. A single 30-mark question could take up to six hours to complete.

Supported throughout by CandLE—an organisation aiding students who use AAC technology—Patrick faced intense physical and mental exhaustion. His headteacher, Ross Martland, and his mother, Jo, had to battle with exam boards to secure accommodations, illustrating the difficulties disabled students encounter in trying to access a level playing field.

Broader Implications and Policy Context

Patrick's experience reflects both the potential and the limitations of the UK government's ambitions for inclusive education under forthcoming Send reforms, which aim to keep children in local mainstream schools with proper support. While Martland supports the moral and values-based framework of these plans, he and other educators caution that proper resourcing and funding are vital to prevent placing unsustainable pressure on schools.

Beyond academics, Patrick has pointed out social hurdles, noting that communication barriers can make forming friendships challenging. Looking ahead, Patrick plans to pursue a university degree in media studies after completing his A-levels.

Practical Implications and Verification

Readers wishing to verify the original report and learn more about the broader policy context surrounding special educational needs in England can review the full coverage published by [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/education/2026/oct/02/patrick-mccabe-success-cheshire-reveals-limits-send-tech).

What is Confirmed vs. Unknown

  • Confirmed: Patrick McCabe passed seven GCSEs using eye-tracking technology, took four months to complete his exams, is now studying A-levels at Fallibroome Academy, and was supported by CandLE and teaching assistants.
  • Unknown: The precise financial costs and long-term resource allocations of the government's upcoming Send reforms remain under discussion and subject to future implementation details.
